sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
July 2026 delivered a deeply bifurcated global equity tape, as two opposing forces — a geopolitical shock from resumed U.S.-Iran hostilities that sent crude oil surging more than **+22%** and a last-session Amazon-led tech earnings rally — nearly cancelled each other out at the index level. The S&P 500 closed the month essentially flat at **7,489.72**, the Nasdaq Composite shed **-3.2%** to **25,373.85** — its worst monthly performance since Q4 2025 — while the Dow Jones Industrial Average eked out a **+0.3%** gain to **52,485.03**, recording its fourth consecutive monthly advance as energy and value names carried the tape.

European indices staged a meaningful divergence, with the DAX gaining **+3%** to close near **25,800**, driven by energy sector outperformance and resilient industrial earnings. The FTSE 100 closed near **10,897** and the CAC 40 near **8,486**, with mixed sectoral outcomes. APAC markets were considerably weaker: Japan's Nikkei 225 declined to **64,362** from June's **70,062** close as Bank of Japan hawkish signals and a Samsung-linked technology rout weighed, while the Shanghai Composite fell a sharp **-6.81%** as U.S. tariff escalation and property sector headwinds compounded.

The month's defining dynamic was the radical re-pricing of geopolitical risk premiums following the July 8 U.S. military strikes on Iranian facilities. The divergence between a resilient Dow — buoyed by energy, industrials, and financials — and a declining Nasdaq encapsulates an equity market in a genuine regime transition: from a narrow, AI-concentration-driven advance into a cross-asset repricing that rewards value, energy, and shorter-duration cash flows over speculative technology multiples.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
US-Iran War Re-Escalation & the Crude Oil Supply Shock -- The single most consequential market event of July 2026 was the U.S. military strike on Iranian nuclear and missile facilities on July 8, which reversed the ceasefire-driven oil price normalization that had been the dominant macro tailwind in June. Brent crude surged more than **+22%** for the month, touching intra-month highs near **$99/bbl** before settling near **$87.84/bbl** by July 31 as naval escorts provided intermittent Strait of Hormuz passage; WTI tracked higher by a comparable **+23%** to **$85/bbl**. Goldman Sachs sharply revised its Q3 2026 Brent forecast upward to **$95/bbl**, reversing the **$80/bbl** target set following June's peace framework.

The oil supply shock delivered an immediate stagflationary impulse to an economy already navigating elevated Federal Reserve vigilance. Airlines, chemical producers, and logistics companies — many of which had rapidly reduced crude hedges on the June ceasefire news — faced severe near-term margin compression with minimal buffer, and sell-side analysts began processing the implications for Q3 2026 earnings guidance. Energy sector equities globally registered their best monthly performance since 2022, with U.S. E&P names and European integrated oil majors posting double-digit monthly gains.

For financial markets, the re-escalation has materially complicated the H2 2026 macro narrative. The Strait of Hormuz — through which approximately a fifth of global oil flows — remains partially disrupted, and any further deterioration in U.S.-Iran negotiations could push Brent back toward or above **$100/bbl**, a threshold that would almost certainly force a Federal Reserve policy response and trigger a more abrupt de-rating of equity multiples. The episode underscores how fragile the June peace dividend proved to be and how quickly structural supply constraints can reassert themselves.

Amazon Blowout & the Big Tech Q2 Earnings Season -- Amazon's July 30 Q2 2026 results delivered one of the most consequential single-stock earnings reports in recent memory: revenue of **$200.6 billion** — the company's first quarter exceeding the **$200 billion** threshold — on earnings per share of **$5.75**, dramatically ahead of the sell-side consensus of **$1.81**. AWS cloud revenue grew **37%** year-over-year to **$42.2 billion**, the fastest rate in 18 quarters, as AI inference workloads and enterprise cloud migrations drove demand materially above expectations. Operating income climbed to **$27.5 billion** from **$19.2 billion** in Q2 2025.

Amazon's beat was the headline event of a broadly constructive earnings season for U.S. mega-cap technology: Microsoft, Meta Platforms, and Apple also reported Q2 figures ahead of consensus, with S&P 500 operating earnings growth for Q2 2026 tracking **+15%** year-over-year. The Amazon-driven surge on July 31 lifted the S&P 500 by more than **+1%** on the final trading day, effectively rescuing the index from a materially deeper monthly drawdown and enabling the Dow to post its fourth consecutive monthly gain.

However, the market's reaction to the broader tech earnings season was notably muted relative to the magnitude of the beats. Amazon guided full-year 2026 cash capex to **$220 billion** — roughly **+50%** above 2025 levels — contributing to a collective hyperscaler AI infrastructure commitment estimated above **$500 billion** across the four major cloud operators. Investors are increasingly pricing in a scenario where AI infrastructure investment will not generate commensurate revenue returns for multiple quarters, a concern that contributed directly to Nasdaq's **-3.2%** monthly underperformance despite a strong earnings season underneath.

Federal Reserve Holds, But September Rate Hike Risk Mounts -- The Federal Reserve's July FOMC meeting produced no policy change, with the committee voting unanimously to hold the federal funds rate at **3.50%–3.75%**, but Chair Kevin Warsh's statement introduced hawkish language that materially shifted terminal rate expectations. The committee removed prior guidance suggesting a neutral policy stance, noting that supply-side inflationary pressures from energy dislocations and tariff pass-through posed upside risk to the **2%** inflation target. CME FedWatch subsequently priced a greater-than-**50%** probability of a **25 basis point** rate hike at the September 2026 FOMC meeting.

U.S. Treasury yields reacted immediately: the 10-year note finished July at **4.75%**, moving **+25 basis points** from the June 30 close, while the 2-year yield climbed to **4.28%**, implying a 10-2 spread of **+47 basis points** as the curve modestly steepened. Real yields on 10-year TIPS moved above **2.3%** — a level that historically creates meaningful headwinds for equity multiples in technology and other long-duration sectors. Rate-sensitive sectors including REITs, utilities, and consumer staples underperformed the broader index materially on a monthly basis.

For asset allocators, the prospect of a hiking cycle resumption in September 2026 — barely one quarter after June's hawkish pivot had been absorbed — introduces the risk of a more aggressive tightening trajectory than consensus had assumed entering H2. The Fed's central dilemma remains unchanged: an energy-driven supply shock is inherently stagflationary, punishing real growth while simultaneously demanding a policy response that further tightens financial conditions. How the committee navigates this trade-off will be the defining macroeconomic question for the remainder of 2026.

Tariff Escalation, China Underperformance & EM Pressure -- The Trump administration's trade policy intensified in July, with new tariff measures taking effect on goods from 60 trade partners covering more than **99%** of U.S. trade, creating visible supply-chain disruption signals across manufacturing PMI surveys globally. The complex and overlapping tariff structure — partly reconstructed following a Supreme Court ruling that voided some measures under the original legal authority — drove an uptick in corporate guidance withdrawals as compliance teams at multinationals struggled to operationalize the framework in time for Q3 planning.

China bore the sharpest immediate cross-asset impact: the Shanghai Composite fell **-6.81%** — its worst monthly decline in over a year — as escalating trade restrictions intersected with below-consensus Q2 GDP growth data and continued property sector deleveraging. The PBOC's targeted reserve requirement cuts provided partial cushion but failed to stem capital outflows that pressured the CNY and weighed on broader emerging market currency performance. The Caixin Manufacturing PMI export orders sub-index contracted for a second consecutive month, validating the earnings-risk narrative for China-exposed multinationals.

For global portfolio managers, China's underperformance raises fundamental questions about the durability of the APAC growth narrative that had underpinned allocation into Hang Seng and A-shares earlier in 2026. Several major investment banks downgraded their China equity outlooks to underweight during July, citing the combination of tariff uncertainty, property sector overhang, and reduced domestic policy space. The contrast with European equities — where the DAX gained **+3%** on energy strength and resilient industrial orders — encapsulates a global growth rotation that strategists expect to persist through Q3 and Q4.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
U.S. equity performance in July 2026 was defined by an increasingly stark divergence between value-oriented large-caps and growth-heavy technology names. The Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced **+0.3%** to close at **52,485.03**, driven by energy sector leadership — major E&P and integrated oil names each gained double digits on the crude oil surge — alongside financial sector resilience and healthcare stability. The S&P 500 ended essentially flat at **7,489.72**, masking significant cross-sectional dispersion; equal-weight S&P 500 outperformed the cap-weight version materially as energy and industrials dominated while mega-cap technology weighed on aggregate index returns.

The Nasdaq Composite bore the heaviest losses, declining **-3.2%** to **25,373.85** as a wave of de-risking in long-duration growth names preceded and initially overshadowed the Q2 earnings season. Concerns centered on AI capital expenditure sustainability — the collective capex guidance from Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta for 2026 exceeded **$500 billion** — and whether infrastructure investment at this scale could be justified by near-term AI revenue returns. Philadelphia Semiconductor Index names were particularly volatile, oscillating around critical TSMC and Nvidia guidance updates that shaped investor appetite for the AI infrastructure theme.

The decisive turning point came on July 31 when Amazon's Q2 2026 blowout — **$200.6 billion** in revenue and AWS growth of **37%** — catalyzed a broad market rally that lifted the S&P 500 by more than **+1%** on the final trading day. The month's outcome — a fourth consecutive winning month for the Dow, Nasdaq's worst month in over a year, and an S&P 500 that ended flat despite extraordinary intra-month volatility — is the clearest signal yet that equity leadership is rotating away from the mega-cap growth complex toward value, energy, and dividend-yielding sectors.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity markets outperformed their U.S. growth-heavy counterparts in July 2026, with energy sector strength and resilient industrial earnings driving positive regional returns. The DAX gained **+3%** to close near **25,800**, led by integrated oil majors, chemicals, and machinery exporters that benefited from the crude surge even as trade policy uncertainty cast a shadow over export-oriented manufacturing. The FTSE 100 and CAC 40 showed more mixed outcomes, closing near **10,897** and **8,486** respectively, with energy names offset by weakness in consumer discretionary, automotive, and technology components.

The re-escalation of U.S.-Iran hostilities proved a structural tailwind for European large-cap indices given their significantly heavier energy sector weighting relative to U.S. benchmarks. BP, Shell, TotalEnergies, and ENI collectively gained double-digit percentages in July, accounting for a disproportionate share of regional outperformance. European industrials also benefited from continued defense spending momentum, as NATO member nations accelerated procurement in response to fresh geopolitical instability, providing incremental revenue tailwinds for Airbus, Rheinmetall, and BAE Systems.

Not all European sectors benefited equally: automotive stocks declined on U.S. tariff uncertainty, with German OEMs particularly exposed to the new trade framework covering **99%** of U.S. trade partners that took effect in July. European banks were mixed — the prospective September Fed rate hike provided a net interest margin tailwind for cross-border operations, but higher oil-driven inflation raised concerns about consumer loan quality in Southern Europe. The ECB maintained its policy rate unchanged at its July meeting, noting it would monitor energy price pass-through before adjusting its own path.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asia-Pacific equity markets delivered a strongly divergent performance in July 2026, with the region's two largest economies — Japan and China — moving in opposite directions under distinct but intersecting macro pressures. Japan's Nikkei 225 declined to **64,362** from June's **70,062** close — a monthly retreat of roughly **-8%** — as the Bank of Japan's increasingly hawkish signals on potential rate normalization strengthened the yen and compressed the export-earnings multiple that had underpinned the index's exceptional year-to-date advance. A Samsung-driven technology rout in Korean markets spilled into Japanese semiconductor and electronics names, adding a further layer of pressure to an already-fragile sentiment backdrop.

China was the clear regional laggard. The Shanghai Composite fell **-6.81%** — its worst monthly decline in over a year — pressured by U.S. tariff escalation covering **99%** of trade partners, consecutive months of Caixin manufacturing PMI export-order contraction, and continued property sector deleveraging. The Hang Seng tracked broadly lower as well, weighed by declines in China technology and consumer names. The PBOC cut the reserve requirement ratio for select banks mid-month but refrained from broader stimulus, disappointing markets that had been pricing more aggressive easing given the deteriorating trade and growth outlook.

The Bank of Japan's July meeting was the most closely watched event for the region: while the BOJ refrained from an immediate rate hike, revised policy language strongly implied a normalization move before year-end 2026. USD/JPY approached **161** as the initial yen-strengthening impulse proved insufficient to sustain appreciation against a dollar still supported by higher U.S. yields. The prospective narrowing of the U.S.-Japan rate differential is a structural shift for global carry trades, regional FX volatility, and the relative returns of Japanese equity investors who have benefited from yen-denominated hedging windfalls through the first half of the year.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
Currency markets in July 2026 were shaped by the interaction of three competing forces: geopolitical risk-driven demand for U.S. dollar safe-haven assets, the inflationary impulse of higher crude oil prices, and growing expectations of a September Fed rate hike that periodically supported the greenback. The DXY traded in a relatively tight range, touching an early-July high near **101.39** before settling back to **100.5** by month-end as the immediate Hormuz risk premium partially faded and the Fed's July statement provided no additional catalyst to break the recent trading range.

EUR/USD held near **1.14**, as the euro benefited from energy sector terms-of-trade improvement in European current accounts while the ECB's July hold limited rate-differential widening that had pressured the pair in June. GBP/USD traded near **1.33**, with sterling supported by resilient UK labor market data and the Bank of England's continued hold. The most significant developed-market FX move was in the Japanese yen: USD/JPY approached **161** as BOJ hawkish signals proved insufficient to drive sustained yen appreciation against a dollar still supported by higher U.S. real yields, while yen carry-trade positioning remained crowded and vulnerable to further BOJ language shifts.

Emerging market currencies experienced broad-based pressure in July, with CNY, INR, and MXN all weakening as tariff escalation covering **99%** of U.S. trade partners triggered capital outflows from EM assets. The Chinese yuan's controlled but persistent depreciation reflects official tolerance for a weaker exchange rate as a partial offset to export volume losses. EM central banks in commodity-importing economies faced a particularly acute policy trade-off: defending currencies against a weak domestic growth backdrop while import inflation from higher energy prices eroded real household purchasing power — a constraint that limits their ability to ease policy in response to slowing growth.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
July 2026 was defined almost entirely by the crude oil market and the geopolitical events that drove it. Brent crude surged **+22.74%** for the month to close near **$87.84/bbl** on July 31 — its best monthly performance in over two years — following U.S. military strikes on Iran on July 8 that triggered immediate Strait of Hormuz shipping disruptions and reversed the post-ceasefire equilibrium near **$75/bbl** that had briefly prevailed in late June. WTI crude advanced a comparable **+23.46%** to end near **$84.67/bbl**, with both benchmarks touching intra-month highs near **$99/bbl** before retracing as U.S. naval escorts and alternative routing partially alleviated the supply shock.

Gold gained **+0.5%** to settle near **$4,042.97/oz** at July 31 — a near-record level supported by safe-haven demand, rising inflation expectations, and a broadly stable dollar. The relative underperformance of gold versus crude oil reflects the competing headwind of higher real Treasury yields: with 10-year TIPS yields above **2.3%**, the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold remains elevated. Copper gained **+5.92%** in July to **$6.49/lb**, supported by a combination of AI data center construction demand driving electrical wire and transformer requirements, and supply disruptions from South American mining regions that tightened physical market balances.

The commodity complex delivered its strongest aggregate monthly performance in over two years, driven overwhelmingly by energy. For corporate earnings, the crude oil move has two distinct second-order effects: it represents a material earnings acceleration for energy producers globally, while simultaneously imposing margin compression on airlines, shipping companies, chemical producers, and consumer goods manufacturers that will likely crystallize in Q3 2026 guidance downgrades. The IEA revised its global oil demand forecast for H2 2026 upward by **0.4 million barrels per day**, assuming sustained supply disruption will require strategic petroleum reserve releases by consuming nations to partially compensate.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
U.S. Treasury yields moved meaningfully higher in July, as oil-driven inflation expectations and rising September rate-hike probability combined to push the curve upward across tenors. The 10-year Treasury note finished July at **4.75%**, moving **+25 basis points** from the June 30 close, while the 2-year yield settled at **4.28%** — resulting in a 10-2 spread of **+47 basis points** as the curve modestly steepened. The steepening reflects a market increasingly pricing near-term rate stability alongside elevated long-term inflation risk from structural energy market disruption.

The Federal Reserve's decision to hold at **3.50%–3.75%** was widely expected, but Chair Warsh's commentary on supply-side inflationary pressures from crude oil and tariff pass-through signaled a materially higher bar for any near-term rate reduction. Fed funds futures ended July pricing a greater-than-**50%** probability of a **25 basis point** hike at the September 2026 FOMC meeting — a dramatic reversal from the cut expectations prevailing in May. This shift in terminal rate expectations drove a meaningful widening in 30-year mortgage rates, further dampening the housing market recovery that had begun in Q1 2026.

Credit markets showed early signs of stress: investment grade corporate spreads widened by **+15 basis points** and high yield by **+40 basis points** over the course of the month, as energy-driven inflation and rate-hike risk combined to pressure leveraged balance sheets and increase refinancing risk for lower-rated issuers. European sovereign spreads — particularly Italian BTPs — widened modestly on oil price inflation pass-through concerns, while UK Gilts tracked Treasuries higher in yield. For fixed income allocators, the July repricing suggests a regime where neither the short nor the long end provides a clear safe harbor, and active duration management will be a key performance differentiator through H2 2026.
